stimulus.text:
| Place | Action | What it did |
|---|---|---|
| Vermont | 1777 constitution | Slavery banned outright |
| Pennsylvania | 1780 law | Children born after March 1, 1780, free at age 28 |
| Massachusetts | 1783 court decisions | Slavery ended under the 1780 state constitution |
| Connecticut | 1784 law | Children born after March 1, 1784, free at age 25 |
| Rhode Island | 1784 law | Children born after March 1, 1784, free at 18 (girls) or 21 (boys) |
| New York | 1799 law | Children born after July 4, 1799, free at 28 (boys) or 25 (girls) |
| Northwest Territory | 1787 ordinance | Slavery banned in the territory |
stimulus.source_note: Compiled from state constitutions, statutes, and court decisions, 1777-1799. Public record.

books.section: Topic 3.6 The Influence of Revolutionary Ideals, A. The Call for Egalitarianism

stem: Pennsylvania's rule freeing children at age 28 best shows that gradual emancipation was designed to

options.text: Free every enslaved person in the state on the day the law passed
options.misconception: The law freed no living enslaved person at once; it freed only children born after 1780, and only at 28.

options.text: End slavery at once by paying owners for their enslaved workers
options.misconception: Pennsylvania paid owners nothing; the age-28 wait was the payment, in years of labor, not in money.

options.text: Protect owners' property by keeping children in service until adulthood
Send freed children to settle in the Northwest Territory
options.misconception: The law says nothing about the Territory; the children stayed in Pennsylvania, working for their mothers' owners.

rationales.C: A child born in 1780 worked until 1808, so the owner kept nearly a lifetime of labor. Background: the 28-year wait compensated owners for the cost of raising the child.
rationales.A: No one alive in 1780 was freed by the law; only children born after it, and only at 28, ever went free.
rationales.B: No payment was made; the compensation was the child's labor until adulthood, not money from the state.
rationales.D: The Territory appears in a different row; Pennsylvania's law keeps the children where they were born.
rationales.general:
1. Read the rule. Children born after March 1, 1780, go free at 28.
2. Count the years. A child born in 1780 labors until 1808 — nearly a working life.
3. Ask who gains. The owner keeps the labor; freedom waits a generation.
Remember: a waiting age is a price — ask who pays it and who collects it.
